judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional preamble naming the parties, the Effective Date and the employee's address; nothing in it carries two reasonable meanings beyond the OCR noise.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It names Ajuba Solutions (India) Pvt Ltd alone as 'the Company', yet Section 2.4 keys the principal economic benefit to transactions by MiraMed and Section 7.8 sweeps in the Parent, a mild but real mismatch of contracting parties.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Business' is defined by an open-ended 'including but not limited to' list plus 'such other entities serviced by the Company at any time', so the catch-all's reach against the enumerated services is genuinely uncertain (classic 1.3).
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The term drives the scope of 'Company Technology' (1.2) and the assignment duty in 4.1 ('relating in any way to the Business'), so its breadth matters, but nothing in those clauses contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition of 'Company Technology' turns on ideas 'known to the Employee' as a result of or through his employment 'and which relate to the Business' — both the knowledge trigger and the relatedness test are vague boundaries a court would have to draw.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 4.1 covers matter 'relating in any way to the Business' that Employee 'conceived, developed or acquired', a wider formula than this definition, leaving the operative assignment and the definition imperfectly aligned.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'All information, in whatever form, regarding the Company and the Business' followed by a nine-item 'without limitation' list is the archetypal general-versus-specific problem, and the general phrase has no limiting qualifier such as non-public or proprietary.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with Article 3's confidentiality covenant and its public-domain exception, which cabins the breadth somewhat; no operative provision contradicts the definition.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'A client of the Company' is short but unremarkable; the only slack is whether past or prospective clients count, which the Confidential Information definition handles separately.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The defined term 'Customer' appears nowhere else in the operative text (no non-solicitation clause uses it), so it is an orphan definition — untidy but not a source of conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A fixed end date of December 31, 2013 subject to earlier termination under Article 6 is definite on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 6.1 adds termination on consummation of a Liquidity Event and Section 6.4 measures severance by 'the remainder of the Term', so the Term's end date is load-bearing but consistently used.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A standard calendar-year fiscal year definition with a fallback for a changed fiscal year; the only defect is OCR damage to '12-month period'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: 'Fiscal Year' is not invoked by any operative provision (bonus and severance run off Base Salary and the Term), so it neither conflicts with nor supports anything.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition breaks off mid-sentence ('any corporation, company, partnership, other entity or ...'), an incompleteness that would matter only if the term were used.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: 'Person' does not appear in any operative covenant of the agreement other than the representations in 5.1, so the truncation causes no live inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Duties are fixed by reference to Schedule 2.1 and to what a President 'customarily' performs, and the exclusivity bar on 'any other business or professional activity' whether or not during business hours is broad and undefined at the edges.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 6.2(b) makes failure to perform 'consistent with the provisions of Schedule 2.1' a Cause ground and 6.4 makes diminution of duties 'as outlined in Section 2.1' Good Reason, so an absent or vague Schedule 2.1 ripples through the termination scheme.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Base Salary and the US$18,800 Allowance are stated numerically, but the reservation that benefits 'may be modified or discontinued at the sole discretion of the Company' sits uneasily with the promise of participation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 6.4 treats 'a breach by the Company of the compensation and benefit provisions' as Good Reason, so the sole-discretion power to cut benefits and the Good Reason trigger pull against each other.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional reimbursement clause; 'reasonable out-of-pocket expenses' subject to Company policies is qualified but not genuinely two-meaninged.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing elsewhere — including the Cause and severance provisions — addresses expenses, so no relational tension appears.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The tiers do not cohere arithmetically — 2.73% at US$180M yields about US$4.91M, the middle band is a flat US$5M, and the top band drops to 2.3% (US$4.6M at US$200M) — a numerical discontinuity that reads as a mechanical error, compounded by the release condition 'in the form attached hereto' where no form appears.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It requires the Employee to be 'employed by the Company at the time of consummation' while Section 6.1 terminates employment 'upon the consummation of a Liquidity Event', and Section 2.4(d) adds a further condition of remaining employed when deferred payment is due; that is a direct clash.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The 1.75% tail payment is stated plainly, but it says nothing about the tiering in 2.4(a) or whether the release condition applies, leaving its interaction with the main formula open.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It cross-refers to Cause and Good Reason 'as defined in Section 6.4', yet Cause is defined in 6.2 and not 6.4 — a mis-citation that a court would have to correct, and it also has to be squared with 2.4(a)'s employment condition and 6.1.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Limb (ii) strings together three transactions followed by the qualifier 'in which Tony Mira and members of his immediate family ... will not own at least 50%', and whether that qualifier modifies all three or only the merger is a genuine syntactic ambiguity, aggravated by the carve-out for MiraMed Revenue Group.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The definition is the trigger for the payments in 2.4(a)–(b) and for automatic termination under 6.1, so its scope drives the whole bonus scheme; I found no flat contradiction, only dependence.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Total amount of cash and fair market value of other property paid or payable (including amounts paid into escrow)' plus add-backs for debt, repurchases and dividends invites dispute over what counts, and the clause ends by tacking on an unrelated employment condition for deferred payments.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: That embedded condition — payment 'conditioned on you remaining as an employee ... at the time that payment is due' — cannot be reconciled with Section 6.1's automatic termination on consummation of the Liquidity Event that triggers the payment.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The mechanics of currency conversion and marketable-securities averaging are precise, but the clause repeatedly uses the capitalised term 'Transaction', which the Agreement never defines.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Everywhere else the operative trigger is a 'Liquidity Event' (2.4(a)–(c), 6.1), so a reader must equate 'Transaction' with 'Liquidity Event' by inference rather than by the text.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The exception list is enumerated (a)–(d) with the last limb cut off at 'to the extent disclosure is', and the covenant bars provision of information 'to any entity' — a word narrower than 'person', which may or may not reach individuals.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits with the broad definition in 1.3 and with 3.3's reciprocal duty on the Company; the public-domain and rightful-receipt exceptions harmonise with the definition rather than contradicting it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional acknowledgement-and-return covenant triggered by termination of employment; the obligations (return, delete, destroy) are concrete.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It mirrors 4.2 for Company Technology and depends on the 1.3 definition, and Section 7.7 makes survival of such duties plausible; no conflicting provision surfaced.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The single exception 'except for legitimate business purposes' is an undefined, one-sided escape hatch that could swallow the Company's confidentiality promise — the kind of vague term a court must construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Employee's own confidentiality duty in 3.1 has narrowly drawn exceptions while the Company's has this open one; the asymmetry is notable but not a contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Upon the Company's request ... Employee shall assign' is a promise to assign rather than a present assignment, and 'relating in any way to the Business' together with 'conceived, developed or acquired' is deliberately open-ended.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The definition of Company Technology in 1.2 is narrower (matter known to the Employee through employment and relating to the Business), so the operative assignment reaches further than the defined term it purports to cover.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A straightforward return-and-delete obligation for Company Technology on termination; the duties are concrete and time-fixed.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It parallels 3.2 and depends on the 1.2 definition of Company Technology, whose vagueness is the real issue; nothing in Article 4 or 7 contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A representation carved into three enumerated categories with an 'except ... as disclosed to the Company in writing' qualifier; the categories are specific and the exception is definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overlaps with 5.2's broader no-violation representation, which covers the same ground more generally, but the two are cumulative rather than inconsistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A standard no-conflict representation with an 'including, without limitation' tail that merely illustrates the general obligation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits comfortably beside 5.1 and the Article 3 and 4 covenants; I found no provision it contradicts.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause lists three triggers but points to 'the events set forth in Sections 6.4 through 6.5', silently omitting termination for Cause (6.2) and death or Disability (6.3) — a drafting slip that changes what the sentence covers.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Making employment terminate automatically 'upon the consummation of a Liquidity Event' cannot be squared with 2.4(a), which pays only an Employee 'employed by the Company at the time of consummation', nor with 2.4(d)'s deferred-payment employment condition.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The Cause list mixes specifics (fraud, felony conviction) with elastic terms such as 'conduct causing the Company or its subsidiaries substantial public disgrace or disrepute' and 'gross misdemeanor', and grants a fifteen-day cure for conduct much of which is incapable of cure.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It measures performance against Schedule 2.1 and promises Base Salary 'and Bonus' earned pro rata, yet 'Bonus' is nowhere defined and Schedule 2.1 is not part of the instrument, leaving 6.2 dependent on materials the contract does not supply.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Disability' is given a quantified test (120 days in any 240), but the payment limb — Base Salary 'but not any Bonus' for the remainder of the calendar year — uses the undefined term 'Bonus' and is textually mangled at the operative point.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 6.1 does not list 6.3 among the events causing termination, and 7.4 makes the Agreement binding on heirs and personal representatives while 6.3 denies the estate anything after death; both are frictions with this clause.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Severance is 'the Base Salary and Bonus' that would have been paid for the remainder of the Term, but 'Bonus' is never defined — whether it captures the Liquidity Event Contingent Payout is precisely the sort of term a court must construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It gives the Employee a right to terminate 'for Good Reason or for any other reason pursuant to this Section 6.4', which overlaps and conflicts with 6.5's separate no-severance resignation route, and it is the Cause/Good Reason definition mis-cited by 2.4(b).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause is definite about notice and payment, though letting the Company choose the effective date of the Employee's own resignation (up to thirty business days out) is an unusual allocation of control.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 6.4 already lets the Employee terminate 'for any other reason' with full severance, so 6.5's bare-pay-through resignation right for 'any reason' cannot be reconciled with it without reading one of them down; the chosen date also shifts the 2.4(b) twelve-month window.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard headings clause; its meaning is single and mechanical.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with the rest of Article 7 and creates no tension with any operative term.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Only a fragment of the severability clause survives in the text, but on its ordinary terms it is boilerplate with one meaning.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing in Articles 2 through 6 depends on or contradicts severability; it would matter only if some covenant were struck down.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional no-waiver clause limiting any waiver to the specific instance and purpose; the wording is standard even in fragmentary form.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coexists with the cure and notice mechanics in 6.2 and 7.5 without contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The permitted assignments are enumerated in closed terms ('only (a) ... or (b) ...'), which is definite, though 'shall become a subsidiary of another entity' overlaps oddly with the merger limb.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The listed events largely coincide with Liquidity Events under 2.4(c), which under 6.1 end employment altogether, so the assignment machinery and the automatic-termination rule pull in different directions; it also binds heirs whom 6.3 cuts off.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A routine notice clause listing the permitted delivery methods and deeming delivery; the mechanics are clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Company's notice address is given as Ajuba International LLC / MiraMed Global Services in Michigan although the contracting Company under the preamble is Ajuba Solutions (India) Pvt Ltd, a mismatch of entity that could matter to notices under 6.2 and 6.5.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One sentence subjecting all payments to withholding 'as required by Indian law'; the rule is specific, if narrow.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Contingent Payout under 2.4 is denominated in US dollars and tied to MiraMed, a US parent structure, so confining withholding to Indian law leaves the treatment of that payment unaddressed.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Survival is limited to 'the ongoing provisions of this Agreement, which shall survive ... in accordance with their terms' — but which provisions are 'ongoing' is nowhere identified, an open-textured phrase a court would have to fill in.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No clause in Articles 3, 4 or 7 states its own survival period (3.1 says 'at any future time', 7.12 says 'and thereafter'), so the cross-reference to 'their terms' has little to work with.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A standard integration and no-oral-modification clause; the acknowledgement that the Employee is party to no other employment agreement is definite, though the tail of the clause is garbled.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 2.4(a) expressly contemplates 'prior agreements entered into by you and the Company or MiraMed' whose amounts the Contingent Payout replaces, which is hard to square with a clause superseding all prior agreements between the Company, Parent and Employee.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional denial of third-party rights, though the text is fragmentary and the capitalised 'Parties' is not a defined term in Article 1.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: MiraMed and the Parent are non-signatories whose transactions and benefits pervade 2.4, so a clause denying rights to anyone but the Parties sits awkwardly with a bonus measured by and payable on a non-party's transaction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Pure boilerplate on counterparts with a single, settled meaning.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It has no interaction with any substantive provision of the instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'No sale, transfer, alienation, assignment, pledge, collateralization or attachment of any benefits' is an enumerated list closed by no catch-all, so its reach is fairly clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 7.4 makes the Agreement binding on and inuring to the parties' heirs and personal representatives, which is in some tension with a flat bar on transfer of benefits; the friction is modest.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Disparage' is undefined and the covenant runs 'during the Employment Term and thereafter' without limit, and the list ends with 'employers', apparently a typographical error for 'employees', which changes who is protected.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 3.3 lets the Company disclose the Agreement 'for legitimate business purposes' and 7.7 leaves survival to 'the ongoing provisions', so the perpetual reach of this clause is only loosely anchored elsewhere.
